name: Kalderon Maw
geological_features: Supervolcanic caldera chains spanning entire continents
Rivers of exposed magma flowing in permanent channels across the surface
Tectonic plate boundaries visible as towering ridges of freshly extruded basalt
specific_features: The Maw — a 900-km-wide caldera complex in continuous eruption for at least ten thousand years
Pyroclastic storm cells that circle the equator in a permanent belt of fire and ash
Obsidian spire formations reaching 12 km in height where magma has flash-cooled in the upper atmosphere
description: Kalderon Maw is a world in perpetual geological agony, its surface a tortured landscape of erupting caldera chains and magma rivers that have never known stillness. The planet's large mass generates enormous tidal stresses from its orbital companions, driving volcanism on a scale that has resurfaced the entire crust multiple times over. Temperatures at the equator exceed four hundred degrees Celsius, and even the cooler polar regions simmer at nearly a hundred.

The toxic atmosphere is a choking soup of sulfur dioxide, carbon monoxide, and particulate ash so dense that starlight never reaches the surface. Instead, the world is lit from below — the orange-red glow of magma rivers and eruption plumes providing a hellish illumination that renders the landscape in shades of ember and shadow. The pyroclastic storm belt at the equator generates lightning discharges visible from neighboring planets.

No probe has survived more than forty-seven minutes on the surface, and the three crewed expeditions attempted in the last century all ended in emergency evacuation. Yet the geological data recovered has proven invaluable, revealing tectonic processes that challenge existing models of planetary formation and suggesting that Kalderon Maw may be a world still in the throes of its own violent birth.

The mineral wealth locked in those magma flows is staggering — platinum-group metals and titanium in concentrations that would fund a colonial government for generations. Automated mining proposals have been drafted and shelved repeatedly, each new engineering study concluding that the planet's volatility makes extraction economically viable only if someone is willing to accept catastrophic losses as a cost of doing business.
